“Tuck Everlasting,” a warm-spirited and piercingly touching musical that has nothing flashy or splashy about it.
I feel the same about the future of this enchanting long-shot of a show.
Those who lean that way will be attracted to the tuneful folk-meets-Broadway score, to the solid performances and to the gentle Americana fable with life lessons intimately told.

Still, “Tuck Everlasting” realizes enough of its ambitions to be watchable, and Casey Nicholaw’s staging is full of quiet delights, though his swirly choreography, especially in the show’s climactic ballet, is bland.
But it removes much of the tension from a story filled with agonizing decision-making and enough talk of life and death to keep anyone awake at night.

I can admire several elements here; they just seem slightly misjudged or misaligned.

Charmingly illustrating the stages of a long life marked by love and loss, it achieves a level of subtle artistry that makes everything preceding it seem pedestrian by comparison.
It’s pretty crazy that this story about regret, mortality and big life choices — make that “eternal life or death” choices — could end up so toothless.
I found it to be a musical for the child in someone else.
A polite misfire of a musical about immortality that feels like it goes on forever.

Tuck Everlasting is a real heart-tugger.
The folksy score (by composer Chris Miller and lyricist Nathan Tysen) emphasizes a child’s sense of wonder, along with some tender spots.
Lovely, honest, and ultimately moving, in the ways that matter most, it's what a musical should be.

Wholesome, moral winsomeness will never go out of style, presumably; but a rousing musical it does not make, at least in the case of Tuck Everlasting.
Everything from the costuming to the set to the choreography to the direction plays loud, harsh, and cartoonish doing a disservice to the sincere characters and fine work of the actors.
More than anything else in “Tuck Everlasting,” their lax narrative gives us a real glimpse of just how long forever can be.
Tuck Everlasting will tug at your heartstrings and bring you to your feet at the end.
I will say, hopefully without bias, that I just loved this musical.
As a lovely tale about the joys and dangers that come with being alive, “Tuck Everlasting” makes for a very refreshing experience.
Tuck Everlasting is an imaginative and faithful adaptation of Natalie Babbitt's timeless children's novel that successfully leaves the audience pondering: if you could live forever, would you?
A beautiful set, expert choreography and memorable score aid and brilliant acting aid the storytelling, and it all adds to the play’s fantasy theme.
The big themes of love and immortality provide a framework of ideas upon which this winning production builds smartly.
It’s in its last 15 minutes or so that Tuck Everlasting shakes off its quotidian nature.
It's one of the relatively few takeaways from a show that, despite running about two and a quarter hours, sometimes feels as though it should be called Tuck Neverending.

cn.t: Critics find this family-friendly musical about immortality well-intentioned but modest, praising its touching themes and Casey Nicholaw's poignant choreography while noting its overly sweet tone and forgettable score.
